content:
Offloading keyboard shortcuts to a programmable macro keyboard is the most efficient productivity hack I've ever done.

Keyboard shortcuts exploration journey

I first got into keyboard shortcuts by starting with simple macOS triggers, such as using @@ to automatically type my primary email address, then setting up similar methods for full name, address, phone number, zip code, etc.

After that, I decided to take it a step further by using Keyboard Maestro to set up shortcuts that open several frequently-used folders and applications.

From the desktop to the Downloads folder, and to work-related folders, pressing Fn+F1 to Fn+F6 has become pure muscle memory, allowing me to jump instantly to places that previously required several clicks. Other function keys are used to launch frequently-used applications and websites, as well as to access Keyboard Maestro's clipboard history switcher.

Later, I also started automating parts of my workflow, including opening QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically launching Shure PlusMOTIV whenever a specific USB-C microphone is plugged in.

Soon, I also customized shortcuts for Adobe Audition's tools, settings, and panel configurations, and I even moved some of the keys to the Logitech MX Master to make editing faster.

Taking it to the next level

This setup worked well for a long time, until one day when 9to5Mac's Gui Rambo told me he had bought a small macro keyboard with 12 buttons and 3 knobs. I was immediately intrigued after hearing about it, and I went ahead and bought the same one.

After it arrived, I first realized that setting it up to work properly on macOS required extra effort. Fortunately, this GitHub project helped me handle all the technical details, and with the assistance of ChatGPT, I finally got everything working.

One advantage of this setup is that you can use a custom keyboard to trigger Keyboard Maestro shortcuts without having to memorize them by heart, nor having to compromise on ergonomics.

Moreover, because this keyboard can be configured with up to 3 layers of shortcuts across 12 buttons, and the knobs themselves can also be used as buttons, I can use one mode when working in Adobe Audition and an entirely different mode when operating the system.

When using Adobe Audition, combining this macro keyboard with the MX Master makes switching tools, exporting files (or just exporting specific segments), and applying effects such as normalization, compression, de-reverb, de-essing, ripple delete, etc., so much faster and smoother that it's simply not in the same league as using regular keyboard shortcuts, or even not using shortcuts at all.

On the operating system front, I can switch the same keyboard to another layer to instantly change audio input, adjust volume, adjust screen brightness, mute or unmute the microphone, and quickly open frequently-used folders.

Of course, memorizing all the commands did take a little bit of time, but once you get used to it, it becomes natural much faster than you'd imagine. More importantly, once you've experienced it, you feel like your Mac is broken without it.

Beyond this, macro keyboards also have countless configurations and options—different shapes, sizes, key layouts, knobs, lighting colors, and so on. This path of exploration really seems endless, and if your work involves any repetitive actions (and whose doesn't?), I genuinely recommend you check it out.
